questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a dedicated integration user instead of pointing an integration at a real employee's login?
options: Dedicated integration users are always cheaper from a licensing standpoint
Tying the integration to a human login means it breaks or silently changes access whenever that employee's own status or permissions change, and makes 'who did this' ambiguous during an incident
Real employee logins cannot technically be used for API calls
Salesforce prohibits using any human account for integrations
questions.explain: A dedicated integration user decouples the integration's identity and access from any one human's employment status, role changes, or password resets -- and keeps accountability clear if something goes wrong.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is the most common way an integration user ends up with far more blast radius than it needs?
options: Enabling API Only on its profile
Granting it the System Administrator profile for convenience, so it 'never breaks when something new is added'
Assigning it a narrowly-scoped custom permission set
Giving it a named, accountable owner
questions.explain: A System Administrator profile on an integration user is the most common over-scoping mistake, almost always chosen for convenience rather than because the integration genuinely needs administrative access.

questions.q: What does the API Only User setting accomplish when paired with API Enabled and a narrowly-scoped permission set?
options: It grants the integration user broader object access automatically
It removes the need for any profile or permission set scoping at all
It disables TLS requirements for that specific user
Even if the credential is exposed, the user can't log into the UI and browse around -- it's limited to the API surface the permission set allows
questions.explain: API Only closes off the UI login path entirely, so a compromised integration credential is still confined to API calls within whatever access the profile and permission sets grant -- a smaller surface than a full UI session.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an integration user needs a named owner?
options: Only System Administrators are allowed to own integration users
Named ownership is required before an integration user can be granted API Enabled
Without a named owner, the account tends to become organizational driftwood -- nobody reviews its access, and nobody feels empowered to deactivate it once the integration is retired
Ownership is only a legal formality with no practical effect
questions.explain: A named, accountable owner is what keeps an integration user from quietly outliving its purpose -- someone has to know what it's for, review its access, and be the one who decommissions it when the integration ends.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what should happen to an integration user's lifecycle when the integration it supports is decommissioned?
options: The account should be converted into a human employee's login
Nothing changes -- integration user lifecycle is independent of the integration's lifecycle
The account should be left active indefinitely 'just in case it's needed again'
It should be deliberately deactivated or deleted as part of the decommissioning, rather than left active unused
questions.explain: A credible offboarding step for a decommissioned integration includes deactivating or deleting its dedicated integration user -- leaving unused-but-active access around is exactly the over-retention risk this course warns against elsewhere.
